The Silver pomfret Pampus argenteus attains a maximum recorded total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], a size that situates this species among the larger stromateoids inhabiting the continental shelf waters of the Indo-West Pacific. Adult body mass correspondingly reaches an ultimate wet weight of 4270 grams [Wwi = 4270 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships that describe a steep allometric scaling exponent typical of deep-bodied, laterally compressed fishes. This substantial adult size is achieved over a prolonged growth period, and field surveys across the Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea indicate that a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] represents the thermal regime under which most of the species' somatic development occurs. The ecological implications of such a large body size are evident in its dietary ecology: adult pomfrets are voracious predators of pelagic cnidarians and ctenophores, with occasional inclusion of small fishes and crustaceans. This trophic specialization may constrain the species to warm, productive waters where gelatinous prey is abundant year-round, and it likely contributes to the observed variation in growth rates between different regional stocks.

At the onset of reproductive life, individuals of Pampus argenteus have already attained a substantial portion of their ultimate length, with the total length at puberty recorded at 25.3 cm [Lp = 25.3 cm]. This measurement indicates that females begin vitellogenesis and males commence spermiation once they have reached roughly 42 percent of their maximum body length, a developmental threshold that appears consistent across populations sampled from Kuwait to the South China Sea. The age at which this length is achieved varies with local thermal conditions, but at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], gonadal recrudescence becomes apparent in sub-adults approaching this size threshold. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from individuals captured during the pre-spawning season reveals the onset of oocyte development coincident with the achievement of this length, confirming that puberty is size-mediated rather than strictly age-determined in this species. Such a pattern is common among iteroparous teleosts inhabiting warm, seasonally stable environments, where growth rates can be rapid enough to decouple size and age.

Reproductive output in the Silver pomfret is substantial, with females producing approximately 221894 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 221894 eggs per spawning event] during the peak spawning period, and individual females may release one spawning batch daily [F_R_i = one spawning batch daily]. This high fecundity was recorded in specimens maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] throughout the reproductive cycle, conditions that closely mimic the species' natural thermal habitat during the spawning season. The corresponding daily spawning frequency suggests that individual females may release several batches of eggs over the course of a single reproductive season, a strategy consistent with the asynchronous oocyte development observed in histological sections of gravid ovaries. The high fecundity per event is energetically demanding, and field studies indicate that feeding intensity diminishes during peak spawning, with individuals relying on stored lipid reserves to meet the metabolic costs of gametogenesis. Such trade-offs between current reproductive investment and somatic maintenance are well documented among tropical and subtropical marine fishes.

The early life stages of Pampus argenteus begin with a remarkably small neonate, the wet weight at birth being measured at 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams]. This minute mass corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 1.15 millimeters, calculated from the volumetric relationship for a spherical teleost egg. Pelagic eggs of this size are typical of stromateoid fishes and reflect a developmental strategy in which the yolk reserves must sustain the larva through a relatively brief endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. Hatching occurs within 24 to 36 hours after fertilisation at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], producing a yolk-sac larva that measures roughly 1.8 millimeters in total length. The transition to first feeding is critical, and larval rearing studies have demonstrated that the point of no return is reached approximately three days after hatching if suitable planktonic prey is not available. This narrow window of opportunity for the trophic switch imposes strong selection on spawning timing to coincide with peaks in microzooplankton abundance.

Longevity data for the Silver pomfret indicate a maximum lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years] under natural conditions, with the oldest documented individuals captured at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] in the northern Arabian Gulf. This comparatively short lifespan for a fish of its ultimate length suggests a life history strategy characterized by rapid growth, early maturity, and high reproductive investment — traits that align with the species' position in warm, productive coastal ecosystems where mortality pressure from predators, including larger scombrids and elasmobranchs, is considerable. Age determination based on otolith annuli has validated this maximum age estimate across multiple populations, though some regional variation exists, with individuals from cooler, higher-latitude waters exhibiting slightly slower growth and potentially greater longevity. The trade-off between rapid somatic growth and extended lifespan is evident when comparing Pampus argenteus to its congener Pampus chinensis, which attains a smaller ultimate size but can live several years longer under similar thermal regimes.
